clue.text: Priceless volume with Irish poetry

parts.note: read literally as price-less: something with no price costs nothing
V is the abbreviation for volume, as in book references
Erse is an old name for the Gaelic language of Ireland

explanation.surface: A rare book of Irish poems is too valuable to put a figure on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Priceless' usually means too precious to value; the setter reads it as having no price at all. 'with' simply joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Category and member: this unrhymed style with no fixed metre is one kind of poetry.

clue.text: Reflected about medical group showing sign of caution

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so the two pieces together are read from right to left

parts.note: re means about or concerning, as at the head of a business letter
the BMA is the British Medical Association, the professional body and trade union for UK doctors

explanation.surface: After thinking it over, a doctors' organisation is treading carefully.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reflected' turns the two pieces round as a single run, so REBMA becomes the answer. In the surface the word means thought over, and 'about' looks like an instruction but is one of the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the middle traffic light warns drivers to get ready to stop, a signal urging care.

clue.text: More than one boss presents united front to newsmen after unrest

indicators.note: unrest is disorder, so the letters gathered before these words are thrown into a new arrangement
the front of a word is its first letter, here taken from the word that follows

explanation.surface: Several managers stand shoulder to shoulder before the press once the trouble has died down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after unrest' rearranges the two words after the definition plus the N that 'front to' takes from newsmen. 'presents' looks like a verb joining definition to wordplay, but it is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym in the plural: these officials oversee and direct the work of others, so each is a boss.

clue.text: Safety feature, article I grab desperately

parts.note: a is the indefinite article in grammar

indicators.note: desperate actions are wild and frantic, so the word just before it has its letters thrown about

explanation.surface: In a panic I clutch at the one thing that might keep me safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'desperately' rearranges only the word before it, giving RBAG; the I stays where it is printed. 'article' reads as an object in the surface but is the grammatical kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this cushion inflates in a car crash to protect the occupants, one protective device among many.

clue.text: Jack Tar boards with daughter on front of ship

indicators.note: in an across clue, one thing on another is added to its end, so everything before this word follows the ship's letter
the front of a word is its first letter, here that of the word after it
to board a lodger is to take them in, so the word before it takes the next word's meaning inside

parts.note: taken as written; the capital only serves the sailor's nickname
with can mean and, as in fish with chips
D is the abbreviation for daughter in family trees

explanation.surface: A sailor goes aboard a vessel with his daughter and stands at the bow.
explanation.walkthrough: Jack Tar is a nickname for a British sailor, but 'Jack' alone is the definition, a jack being a ship's flag. 'boards' sends the word for 'with' inside the sailor, and 'on' puts all that, daughter included, behind the letter 'front of' picks.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: a jack is a small flag flown from a ship's bow, and a military or royal flag goes by this name.

clue.text: I'll need air conditioning after day stuck in traffic — raging?

indicators.note: something stuck in a thing is lodged inside it, so the earlier pieces go inside the word that follows

parts.note: to traffic in goods is to deal in them

indicators.note: after says the pronoun and the cooling abbreviation come later than the day, though the clue prints them first

parts.note: Mon is the short form of Monday, one day of the week
only the pronoun I is used; the 'll need simply says what it wants beside it

explanation.surface: A driver fumes in a jam all day and longs for some cool air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after' sends the pronoun and the cooling abbreviation behind the day, and 'stuck in' lodges all three inside a verb for 'traffic', to trade. The question mark admits that the definition is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose synonym: the adjective means frenzied like someone possessed by an evil spirit, hence wild with fury.

clue.text: Origins of Zen inspired one native religious community

indicators.note: a word's origin is where it starts, so take the opening letter of each of the four words that follow

explanation.surface: The beginnings of Zen Buddhism moved a local group of believers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Origins of' takes the first letter of each of the next four words. Zen suggests Buddhism, but the community meant is Jewish or Christian.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the name stands for the Jewish people, or for the Christian church seen as a body of believers.

clue.text: Lower class group of workers losing heart in revolution

indicators.note: a revolution is a turning round, so what is left of the workers' group is read from right to left
the heart of a word is its middle letter, and losing it removes that letter

parts.note: a trade union is an organised group of workers

explanation.surface: A working-class labour organisation grows dispirited during an uprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing heart' takes the middle I from UNION to leave UNON, and 'in revolution' turns that round. The answer is a British label, coined in the 1950s, for speech and manners that are not upper class.
explanation.definitionFit: British idiom: U was 1950s shorthand for upper class, so speech or manners marked as the opposite were socially inferior.

clue.text: He wrote music very badly, almost entirely using un-English instruments

parts.note: ill can mean badly, as in ill-treated or ill-advised

indicators.note: almost means not quite all of the next word, so it loses its final letter

parts.note: all means entirely, as in all alone

indicators.note: the prefix un- means without, so the instruments lose the letter that abbreviates English

parts.note: oboes are woodwind instruments

explanation.surface: A dreadful composer scored nearly everything for foreign instruments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts ALL to AL, and 'un-English' takes the E from OBOES to leave OBOS. Heitor Villa-Lobos was Brazil's best-known composer, so the surface's insult is only a story.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Heitor Villa-Lobos was the leading Brazilian composer of the twentieth century.

clue.text: About end of afternoon, one goes on date, waltzing here?

indicators.note: in an across clue, what goes on something is added at its end, so the first group of pieces follows the date
waltzing is whirling round a ballroom floor, so the letters of the word before it change places
about means around, so the word for one goes round the afternoon's letter

parts.note: an ace is the playing card worth one

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, here that of the word after it

explanation.surface: As the afternoon draws to a close, somebody takes a partner out for a waltz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waltzing' rearranges the word before it into TEAD; 'About' wraps a card worth one round the letter 'end of' picks, and 'goes on' sets that group last. The whole clue paints the occasion 'here' points to.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: the whole clue sets the scene, a late-afternoon social where couples waltz, and the last word points at that occasion.

clue.text: Primate's new plan is rejected

indicators.note: to reject something is to send it back, so the three pieces together are read from right to left

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new, as in NT for New Testament
an aim is a plan or intention

explanation.surface: An archbishop's fresh proposal gets turned down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns the three pieces round as a single run, so NAIMIS becomes the answer. A Primate in the surface is a senior archbishop; the definition wants the zoological kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: as an adjective the word means of or like a monkey or ape, creatures of the zoological order named.

clue.text: After Tasmania, neighbour visits seaside resort quick

indicators.note: a visitor goes into a place, so the two pieces named before this word go inside the resort

parts.note: Brighton is a well-known seaside resort on the south coast of England

indicators.note: After says the neighbour word comes later than the Tasmania piece, the order the clue prints them in

parts.note: Tas is the standard abbreviation for the Australian state of Tasmania
as a verb, to neighbour is to abut, to lie right next to

explanation.surface: Having seen Tasmania, the person next door pops down to the coast for a short break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' keeps the neighbour word behind the Tasmania abbreviation, and 'visits' sends both inside the resort, a town on England's south coast. 'neighbour' is a verb here, and 'quick' means quick-witted.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: the simile describes someone clever and mentally alert, the quick of quick-witted.

clue.text: Hear one sits regularly for artist

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so take every second letter of the three words before it

explanation.surface: Word has it that somebody poses for a painter on a fixed schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly' takes every second letter of 'Hear one sits', starting with the E. Max Ernst was a German surrealist painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Max Ernst, the German-born Dada and surrealist painter, is one such figure.

clue.text: Currently teacher is in distant land, heading off for mountain region

indicators.note: is in says the first two pieces sit inside what remains of the distant land
the heading of a word is its first letter, and off means it is removed

parts.note: Asia is a faraway land mass from a British point of view
now means currently, at the present time
a don is a teacher at a British university, especially Oxford or Cambridge

explanation.surface: A schoolmaster is abroad at the moment, about to set out for the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' takes the first letter from the distant land to leave SIA, and 'is in' places the other two pieces inside it. The region is the mountainous national park of north Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this national park in north Wales holds the country's highest peaks.

clue.text: Female on it after unusually big depression

indicators.note: in a down clue, one piece on another sits above it, so the female letter starts the answer
after says the word it comes below the size abbreviation, though the clue names it first

parts.note: F is the abbreviation for female, as on forms
OS is short for outsize, a British clothing label for very large sizes
SA stands for sex appeal, which it meant in old slang, as in the It Girl

explanation.surface: A woman keeps going despite an exceptionally severe bout of low spirits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' puts the female letter at the top, and 'after' sends the old-slang 'it' below the outsize abbreviation, a British label for very large clothes. The depression is anatomical, a hollow in a bone, not a mood.
explanation.definitionFit: Technical synonym: in anatomy this Latin word names a shallow hollow or pit in a bone.

clue.text: Former film director working with fairy folk trying out new ideas

indicators.note: with only says the two pairs stand side by side; here the fairy folk come ahead of the director

parts.note: ex means former, as in ex-wife
a peri is a fairy of Persian myth, a crossword regular
men are folk, people in general
Jacques Tati was the French director and star of the Monsieur Hulot comedies
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: A retired film-maker teams up with elves and pixies to test some fresh concepts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' joins the two pairs without fixing their order: PERI and MEN go ahead of TATI and ON, all behind EX. Jacques Tati directed the Monsieur Hulot comedies.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: the noun means the process of testing fresh methods to see what happens.

clue.text: French writer upset easy-going clergyman? That's no good

indicators.note: in a down clue, something upset is overturned, so the letters are read from the bottom up
these words say the phrase is to have none of the letter that the next word stands for

parts.note: genial means easy-going and good-natured
G is the abbreviation for good, as in VG on schoolwork
Rev is short for Reverend, a clergyman's title

explanation.surface: A novelist from Paris has offended a relaxed vicar, which is a pity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's no' takes G out of GENIAL REV, and 'upset' turns ENIALREV over to give the answer. The question mark excuses the invented phrase; Paul Verlaine was a French poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: Paul Verlaine was a nineteenth-century Symbolist poet from France.

clue.text: Standing right next to armoured vehicle without top

indicators.note: next to says the two pieces sit side by side, in the order the clue gives them

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right, as in L and R

indicators.note: in a down clue the top of a word is its first letter, and without means it is left off

parts.note: a tank is an armoured military vehicle on tracks

explanation.surface: Someone stands beside a tank whose turret has been blown off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without top' leaves ANK from the vehicle, and 'next to' sets it beside the abbreviation. 'Standing' is a noun here, a person's position, not being on one's feet.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both nouns mean a person's position or status in a hierarchy.

clue.text: At last trade union colleague quits as leader

indicators.note: a leader goes first, so the word for quits moves to the front of the answer

parts.note: two people who are quits are even, neither owing the other
TU is the abbreviation for trade union, as in the TUC, Britain's Trades Union Congress
an ally is a colleague or partner

explanation.surface: Finally a fellow union member steps down from the top job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as leader' sends EVEN to the front although the clue prints it last. 'quits' is the adjective of 'now we're quits', not the verb for resigning.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both adverbials mean in the end, after a long wait.

clue.text: Supporting top dog, having nothing to lose

parts.note: A1, written with I for the figure one, means first-rate or top

indicators.note: to lose says the dog's word gives up the letter that the word before these stands for

parts.note: a dingo is the wild dog of Australia
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone backs the boss because there is no risk in doing so.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to lose' leaves DING once the dog gives up its O. 'top dog' is split in two: 'top' is A1, spelt with a letter I in crosswords, and 'dog' is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both participles mean helping or giving assistance to someone.

clue.text: Composer to play jazz in African country and UK, we've heard

indicators.note: in says the jazz word sits inside the name of the country that follows

parts.note: Benin is a country in West Africa
to jam is to play jazz informally, improvising with other musicians

indicators.note: these words say the country named just before is taken by its sound when spoken, not its spelling

parts.note: the UK is loosely called Britain

explanation.surface: A musician is booked for jazz gigs in Africa and Britain, so the rumour goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the jazz verb inside the country, and 'we've heard' asks for a surname that sounds like Britain. Benjamin Britten was the English composer of the opera Peter Grimes.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this Englishman wrote the opera Peter Grimes and the War Requiem.

clue.text: Begrudges storing papers for tenants

indicators.note: to store something is to keep it inside, so the first word's synonym holds the papers within it

parts.note: to begrudge something is to resent it: she resents the cost
ID is identification, the papers you show to prove who you are

explanation.surface: A landlord grumbles about keeping documents on behalf of the people renting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'storing' puts the papers inside the verb for 'Begrudges'. They are identity papers, not newspapers or files in a cabinet.
explanation.definitionFit: Near-synonym: people renting a property live in it, which makes them its occupants.

clue.text: Chief officer left a ship with sailor aboard finding decent accommodation

indicators.note: someone aboard a ship is inside it, so the sailor's letters go inside the run of pieces before

parts.note: C-in-C is short for Commander-in-Chief, the most senior officer
AB is an able-bodied seaman, a grade of sailor
SS stands for steamship, as in SS Great Britain

explanation.surface: The captain abandoned his vessel, a crewman still on it, and found himself a comfortable berth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'aboard' puts the sailor just after the first letter of the run of four pieces. On an ocean liner this grade sits between first and tourist class, hence 'decent'.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: on an ocean liner this is the middle grade of passenger berth, comfortable without being luxurious.

clue.text: Horse and where it's kept in Bedfordshire town

parts.note: a dun is a horse with a dull greyish-brown coat
a horse is kept in a building of this name

explanation.surface: A horse and its stall can both be found in a market place north of London.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedfordshire is an English county north of London. 'and' and 'in' only join the pieces to the definition; nothing goes inside anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this market centre at the foot of the Chiltern Hills lies in the English county named.

clue.text: I shall need one pound, being short of cash

parts.note: I shall contracts to I'll, written here without its apostrophe
I is the Roman numeral for one
quid is British slang for a pound sterling

explanation.surface: Someone who is broke asks to borrow a pound.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole surface describes the answer's plight, but only the last three words define it. 'need' and 'being' are joining words.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: in finance the adjective describes a person or firm without ready money to hand.

clue.text: One may hold 19, perhaps, we hear?

definitions.note: 19 points to the two-word answer at 19 across; only its first word, the drink, belongs to this definition

indicators.note: these words say the step is to be taken by its sound when spoken, which gives a word spelt differently

parts.note: the second word of the answer at 19 across is dance, and a sashay, a gliding sideways step, is one example

explanation.surface: Rumour has it that somebody may be putting on an afternoon ball.
explanation.walkthrough: 19 across is TEA DANCE, and its two words do separate jobs: the packet may hold tea, while 'we hear' asks for a word that sounds like a dance step, SASHAY.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: this is a small sealed packet, and one filled with tea leaves is a familiar example.

clue.text: Fighter held by captain in Jaws

indicators.note: what is held by a phrase lies inside it, so look for consecutive letters running through the three words that follow

explanation.surface: In the shark film, the boat's skipper restrains a brawler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by' says the answer sits unbroken inside 'captain in Jaws'. The capital on Jaws recalls the shark film and plays no part in the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this was a covert warrior of feudal Japan, trained in martial arts and stealth.

clue.text: Old people flying over Portuguese resort

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning something over stands it on its head, so the two pieces together are read from the bottom up

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old, as in OE for Old English
the RAF is the Royal Air Force, Britain's military flying service

explanation.surface: Pensioners look down from a plane as it passes above a holiday town on the Algarve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' turns the whole run O + RAF upside down, ORAF becoming the answer. 'people flying' are the Royal Air Force, Britain's air arm, not passengers.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: this city on the Algarve coast, with its airport and beaches, is a holiday destination in Portugal.
